implementation_notes: GORM follows the struct: a CompanyID field plus a Company field on the child declares the belongs-to association, and the column named by convention (or by gorm:"foreignKey:...") holds the parent's key; references:... overrides which parent column is written and constraint:OnDelete:CASCADE/SET NULL emits the database-level rule at migration time. The library replaces the mapper - it writes the parent key on save and fills the inner struct on Preload/Joins - so the hand-written form is justified only when the SQL must be visible or the ORM dependency is unwanted.
pitfalls: Preload is a second query per relation; touching u.Company inside a loop without Preload is an N+1 that GORM never warns about.
gorm.Model's soft-delete column means a 'deleted' parent still exists for lookups unless every query scopes deleted_at, so a stale key resolves to an invisible row.
Overriding foreignKey without references makes GORM guess between belongs-to and has-one, and the wrong guess silently changes which column is written.

variants.name: Hand-written mapper with database/sql
variants.idiom_name: database/sql + sql.NullInt64 scan and explicit resolve
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ORM the mapping is explicit: Scan the foreign key column into an int64 (or sql.NullInt64 for a nullable reference), then resolve it with a second query or a JOIN in the same statement. There is no reflection, no implicit fix-up and no hidden second query, which is the point; the cost is that ordering, caching and cycle handling are yours to write.
pitfalls: Every query needs its own Scan list: a renamed or reordered column breaks at runtime, not compile time.
Resolving references in a loop without preparing a batched IN (...) query reintroduces the N+1 the ORM would at least have hidden.
sql.NullInt64 must be mapped deliberately - forgetting .Valid writes 0 as a real reference instead of NULL.
